sit_002:n1.prompt:
You are helping me check where my delayed US visa case stands at the consulate. This is educational guidance, not legal advice.

Goal: get an accurate reading of my consular case status on CEAC, the State Department's Consular Electronic Application Center status tracker at https://ceac.state.gov/CEACStatTracker/Status.aspx, and interpret it honestly.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- Visa type (nonimmigrant or immigrant)
- Embassy or consulate location
- Application ID or case number (from my DS-160 confirmation or interview paperwork)
- Interview date, and any refusal or 221(g) sheet the officer gave me

What to do:
1. Prepare a short checklist with the exact values to enter in the CEAC form: visa type, location, and case identifier. Double-check the format against my confirmation page.
2. CEAC has a captcha, no public API, and government terms of use. Tell me exactly what to enter, then stop for human sign-off. I will solve the captcha and submit the lookup myself. Do not solve the captcha, accept terms, or submit the form for me.
3. After I share the status page, or tell you what it says, interpret it:
   - The status label (for example Administrative Processing, Refused, Issued, or Ready) and the last-updated date.
   - If it is Administrative Processing or a 221(g) refusal, explain plainly that it has no fixed clock and no appeal. Most cases resolve, but some take months. Note that premium processing does not speed up a consular 221(g).
   - Whether the consulate appears to be waiting on documents from me.

Done looks like: a status report I can save, with today's date, the CEAC status, the last-updated date, what it most likely means, any documents the consulate requested, and suggested next levers to discuss. Those levers are immigration counsel, a congressional inquiry with my signed privacy release, and a plan to run the company remotely while I wait.

Report back in under 200 words, and flag anything you are unsure about rather than guessing.

sit_002:n2.prompt:
You are helping me check the status of the USCIS petition behind my US visa, if there is one (for example an I-129 for an H-1B or O-1). This is educational guidance, not legal advice. The goal is to pin down exactly where the petition stands, so I know whether the delay is at USCIS or at the consulate.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- Whether a USCIS petition underlies my visa at all. If not, tell me this step does not apply and that consular status lives in CEAC instead.
- The 13-character receipt number from my I-797 notice (three letters followed by ten digits).
- The petition form type, classification, and filing date.

Then prepare the lookup:
1. Validate the receipt number's format and flag anything that looks mistyped.
2. Give me the official USCIS case status page: https://egov.uscis.gov/casestatus/landing.do. Write out exactly what to enter.
3. Explain that this tracker blocks automated agents. The official machine-access route is the Torch Case Status API, which is limited to approved customers and representatives with regular access. So this one-off check is a manual lookup that I do myself. Do not try to get around the bot wall.
4. Draft an interpretation guide for the status wording I am likely to see (received, approved, RFE issued, transferred, denied) and what each one means for my next move. Mark which results point to a USCIS expedite request or Form I-907 premium processing (if my classification qualifies). Note that premium processing does not speed up a consular 221(g) hold.

At that point, stop for human sign-off. I will run the lookup and paste the status text back to you.

When I share the result, report back with:
- the exact status line and its date
- a plain-English reading of where the petition is stuck, if anywhere
- whether the hold-up is at USCIS or downstream at the consulate
- the two or three most sensible next steps (expedite request, premium processing, immigration counsel, or a congressional inquiry)

This step is done when the current petition status is recorded and interpreted.

sit_002:n3.prompt:
You are helping me figure out exactly where my delayed US visa is stuck so I pick the right next lever. This is educational guidance, not legal advice. The determination is mine (or my immigration counsel's) to make. Your job is to lay the evidence beside the official definitions.

Ask me for anything missing:
- My visa category and the consulate where I interviewed.
- The current status text and last-updated date I see on CEAC (State Department consular status). I will check it myself, because the portal sits behind a bot wall.
- If a petition is involved, the receipt number's status text from the USCIS case status tracker. I will also check that myself.
- Any paper I was handed or emailed after my interview, especially a 221(g) slip, and what it asks for.

Then:
1. Read the State Department's administrative processing page at https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/us-visas/visa-information-resources/administrative-processing-information.html. Summarize what 221(g) administrative processing means: there is no fixed timeline and no appeal, most cases resolve, and some take months.
2. Build a side-by-side table. List each status or document I gave you, then the published definition it matches, then which bucket it points to:
   - (a) 221(g) administrative processing
   - (b) a USCIS petition backlog
   - (c) a missing-document request I can act on now
3. Flag any contradictions or ambiguous wording. Note where a misread would cost weeks. For example, premium processing via Form I-907 can speed a qualifying petition but does not speed a consular 221(g).
4. For each bucket, note which levers the process considers relevant. These are an expedite request against USCIS's published criteria, I-907 where the classification qualifies, immigration counsel, and a congressional inquiry with my signed privacy release. Do not start any of them.

Done looks like: the table, a short paragraph on the most likely bucket with your confidence and reasoning, and a list of questions for counsel. Then stop for human sign-off. I or my counsel will confirm the classification before anything is filed or sent.

sit_002:n4.prompt:
You are helping me draft a USCIS expedite request for my delayed US visa petition. This is educational help, not legal advice. Your job is to build the strongest honest case against USCIS's published expedite criteria. Base it on the official guidance at https://www.uscis.gov/forms/filing-guidance/how-to-make-an-expedite-request. Read that page first and use its current wording.

Ask me for anything below that is missing:
- My receipt number and form type (for example I-129).
- The petition classification.
- Where the case stands right now, from my own check of the USCIS case status tracker.
- My role at the company and what the company does.
- The concrete harm the delay is causing: lost contracts, investor deadlines, payroll at risk, customers waiting, or any emergency or humanitarian facts.
- What documents I can produce to prove each claim.

Then:
1. Map my facts to the published criteria, such as severe financial loss, emergencies or urgent humanitarian reasons, and government interest. Use only the categories the page actually lists. For each one, say plainly whether my facts are strong, weak, or don't apply. Do not stretch weak facts.
2. Draft a concise expedite request narrative, about one page. It should tie each claimed harm to specific dates, dollar amounts, and consequences.
3. Build an evidence checklist that pairs each claim with the document that proves it (contracts, letters, bank statements, a third-party letter), and flag the gaps I still need to fill.
4. Note how the page says to submit an expedite request, in words only.
5. Check whether my classification qualifies for Form I-907 premium processing. Make clear that premium processing does not speed up a consular 221(g) hold.

Do not submit anything to USCIS or contact anyone on my behalf. The final review and submission remain a human step. I may also want immigration counsel to review it.

Report back with:
- the criteria assessment
- the draft narrative
- the evidence checklist with gaps marked
- the submission steps
- a one-line honest read on how strong the case is

sit_002:n5.prompt:
You are helping me decide whether to request USCIS premium processing (Form I-907) for my pending petition, and if so, preparing the filing so I can review and submit it myself. This is educational help, not legal advice. Premium processing speeds USCIS adjudication of the petition only. It does NOT speed a consular 221(g) administrative processing hold, so if my case is stuck at the consulate, tell me plainly that this lever does not apply.

Ask me first for anything missing:
- the form type (I-129 or I-140)
- the classification
- the receipt number
- the current status as I see it in the USCIS case tracker (I will check it myself, because the tracker sits behind a bot wall)
- whether I have immigration counsel or a sponsoring employer who files for me

Steps:
1. Open https://www.uscis.gov/forms/all-forms/how-do-i-request-premium-processing and the linked I-907 page.
   - Confirm from USCIS's current published list whether my classification is designated for premium processing.
   - Note the current filing fee, the processing timeframe USCIS states, and whether I-907 can be filed online or must be mailed for my case.
2. If my classification does not qualify, stop and tell me why, citing the USCIS page.
3. If it qualifies, prepare the filing:
   - Pre-fill every I-907 field you can from my answers.
   - Using your browser, you may walk the online flow up to, but not including, eligibility attestations, payment, and final submission.
   - List any supporting items needed, such as a copy of the receipt notice.
4. Stop for human sign-off. Do not attest, accept terms, enter payment, sign, or submit on my behalf. Those actions are mine, or my attorney's.

Done means I have:
- a clear qualify or don't-qualify answer with the source cited
- a pre-filled field list or draft
- the fee and timeframe
- a checklist of the remaining human actions

Report back in that order, flag any field you were unsure about, and suggest I confirm with counsel before submitting.

sit_002:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare to engage immigration counsel through {{vendor}} about my delayed US visa, specifically my 221(g) administrative processing response and the escalation paths open to me. This is educational support, not legal advice. The engagement itself (privileged calls about my case facts, strategy, and risk tolerance) remains a human step that I will handle. Your job is to make that conversation as efficient as possible.

Ask me for anything missing: my visa classification, consulate and interview date, the date I received the 221(g) notice and what it requested, my CEAC status as I last saw it, any USCIS petition receipt number and tracker status, documents already submitted, and my business deadlines.

Then please:
1. Review {{vendor}}'s own pages and summarize whether filings are handled by licensed attorneys (named lawyers or a stated attorney-of-record model), whether a client portal shows case status and next steps, whether it publishes guidance for my consulate or country, and whether it documents RFE/NOID response work and honest fallbacks such as running the company remotely, interim options in other countries, and what happens after a denial. Flag anything you could not confirm.
2. Draft a one-page case brief for counsel: a timeline, the 221(g) request, what was sent, current CEAC and USCIS tracker status (from my clicks; both portals block bots), and my deadlines.
3. Draft questions for counsel covering: a realistic read of 221(g) (no fixed clock, no appeal), whether an expedite request fits USCIS's published criteria, whether Form I-907 premium processing applies to my petition classification (noting it does not speed a consular 221(g)), whether and when to pursue a congressional inquiry with my signed privacy release, and a plan for running the company remotely while I wait.
4. List the documents I should have ready.

If {{vendor}} has a portal or intake form, use your configured credentials only to read status or pre-fill details. Do not submit anything or schedule anything on my behalf.

Done means: a vendor summary, a case brief, a question list, and a document checklist. Report all four back to me with any gaps clearly marked.

sit_002:n7.prompt:
You are helping me open a congressional inquiry into my delayed US visa case. A congressional caseworker can ask the agency for a status update on my behalf, but only after I personally sign that office's privacy release. This is educational guidance, not legal advice.

Ask me for anything missing:
- My US residential address (ZIP+4 if possible).
- Where the case is stuck: a consulate case (CEAC case number, consulate, interview date, any 221(g) notice) or a USCIS petition (receipt number, form type, filing date).
- Key dates and what I have already tried (expedite request, premium processing, counsel).
- The concrete harm of the delay (business impact, deadlines).

Then please:
1. Use https://www.house.gov/representatives/find-your-representative with my ZIP to identify my House Representative. Find their official website, their district office contact details and their casework or 'help with a federal agency' page. Note whether they use an online casework form or a downloadable privacy release, and which agency they list for my case type (State Department or USCIS).
2. Download or link that office's own privacy release form. Pre-fill every field you can from my details, leaving the signature and date blank.
3. Draft a concise cover letter of no more than one page. It should give a timeline, case identifiers, current status, prior steps taken, the specific request (a status inquiry, and expedite consideration if it fits the published criteria) and my contact info. Be honest that 221(g) administrative processing has no fixed clock and no appeal.
4. Assemble a submission checklist: the release, cover letter, notices or receipts, passport bio page if requested, and the office's preferred submission method.

Done looks like a ready packet plus a short report covering my representative and district office, the submission method, the pre-filled release, the draft letter, the checklist and any open questions.

Then stop for human sign-off. Do not sign, date, or submit the release or the inquiry on my behalf. I will review, sign and send it myself.

sit_002:n8.prompt:
You are helping me set an honest plan B while my US visa is delayed: running my company remotely from my current country until the visa clears. Deciding to adopt this plan, and agreeing it with my team, remains a human step. You prepare the thinking and drafts. I make the call and have the conversations.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- My current country and time zone.
- Where the case is stuck (consulate per CEAC, or petition per the USCIS case status tracker) and the latest status I saw. I check those portals myself.
- Any open levers: an expedite request, premium processing, immigration counsel, or a congressional inquiry.
- My team's locations and time zones, key upcoming commitments (customer meetings, fundraising, hires, board dates), and anything that assumes I'm physically in the US.

Then draft a one-to-two-page remote operating plan covering:
1. **Timeline framing.** Administrative processing has no fixed clock and no appeal. Most cases resolve, but some take months. Plan for a range (weeks, a few months, longer) with a review checkpoint for each.
2. **Operations.** Meeting cadence and overlap hours across time zones, who covers US-only tasks (in-person meetings, signatures, banking or office matters), and how decisions get made while I'm away.
3. **Commitments at risk.** List each one with a proposed remote alternative or a delegate.
4. **Hiring and people.** Note what depends on my presence and what can proceed remotely.
5. **Risks and open questions** to raise with immigration counsel. Flag them only. Do not give legal or tax conclusions; this is educational guidance, not legal advice.
6. **Communication.** A short, factual draft note to my team (and optionally to investors) explaining the delay and the plan, with no promised dates.

Done looks like this: a draft plan, a draft team note, and a list of questions for counsel, all ready for my review. Report back with those three items plus a short list of decisions only I can make.

sit_002:n9.prompt:
You are helping me through a delayed US visa while I wait for government action. This step is a wait: a consulate (CEAC case) or USCIS (petition) has to act, and neither runs on a fixed clock. Consular 221(g) administrative processing has no set timeline and no appeal. Most cases resolve, but some take months. Treat this as educational support, not legal advice.

Ask me first for anything missing: whether the case sits with the consulate (CEAC) or USCIS, my case or receipt number, the date processing began, any levers already pulled (expedite request, Form I-907 premium processing, immigration counsel, congressional inquiry), and my last recorded status.

What the agent can do:
1. Build a simple weekly status log with these columns: date checked, portal (CEAC or USCIS case status tracker), status text as I report it, and any change or request received.
2. Set a recurring weekly reminder for me to check status. Both CEAC and the USCIS tracker sit behind bot protection, so checking them yourself or scripting them is not an option. The status check itself remains a human step. I click through and paste the status text back to you.
3. Each time I report back, compare the new status with the previous entry and flag any change. Treat any document request as urgent and draft a reply checklist for it.
4. Keep a short follow-up list. Include dates for chasing counsel or my congressional office if they are involved. Note when continued silence might justify revisiting an expedite request. Remember that premium processing does not speed up a consular 221(g).
5. Keep Plan B visible: running the company remotely from my current country while I wait.

The government's decision and timing remain a human step outside both our control. Do not promise outcomes or timelines.

Done looks like this: the log exists, the weekly reminder is set, and the latest status is recorded. Each week, report back in three lines: current status, change since last check (yes/no and what), and recommended next action, if any.
